clue.text: Winger maybe, balanced in part furthest from finishing

parts.note: in rugby a winger is one of the backs
straight means level or even, as balanced accounts are

explanation.surface: A sports report on a winger who is a steady, balanced player.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Winger' suggests a bird or a footballer on the wing; it is just an example of a back.
explanation.definitionFit: On a racetrack the back straight is the stretch opposite the finishing line, the farthest point from home.

clue.text: 'Strain every sinew'? Objection limits American refrain (8, three words)

indicators.note: to limit something is to hem it in, so one word is placed around the others

parts.note: a 'but' is an objection, as in 'no buts'
standard abbreviation
a tag is a refrain or recurring phrase

explanation.surface: An objector cuts short an American song's refrain, urging the singers to give it everything.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks and question mark flag that the definition is a phrase in quotes; the answer is written as three words.
explanation.definitionFit: To bust a gut is an idiom for making an enormous effort, the same as straining every sinew.

clue.text: Rattle-trap achieving constant speed

parts.note: c is the symbol for a constant in physics, notably the speed of light
rate means pace or speed

explanation.surface: A clapped-out old banger somehow keeps up a steady speed.
explanation.definitionFit: A crate is slang for a decrepit old car or plane, a rattling wreck of a vehicle.

clue.text: Safe as in US, set out protected by Labour leader

indicators.note: protected by means held safely inside, so the rearranged letters go within the leader's name

parts.note: Keir Starmer leads the British Labour Party

indicators.note: set out here means laid out differently, so the three letters of set are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A British party leader guards something kept secure, American style.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer leads Britain's Labour Party; 'protected by' means his name wraps round the rearranged letters. 'Safe' is the noun, a strongbox, not the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: In American slang a keister was a safe or strongbox, as well as a suitcase or the buttocks.

clue.text: Rest dithering around, one heads north making way across border

indicators.note: around places the jumbled letters on either side of what follows
something dithering cannot settle, so these letters are unsettled into a new order

parts.note: the word rest rearranged
a means one, as in 'a single'

indicators.note: the head of a word is its opening letter, so only that letter is kept

parts.note: the first letter of north

explanation.surface: A traveller dithers about resting before heading north to cross the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Across border' means north of the English border: TRANSE is a Scots word for a passage or corridor.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots a transe is a passage or lobby inside a house, a way through from one part to another.

clue.text: Derelict, touching failure

parts.note: re means concerning or touching on
a miss is a failure to hit

explanation.surface: A derelict building with a touching story of failure.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Derelict' looks like a noun or an adjective for a ruin; here it means neglectful of duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Derelict can mean negligent, as in dereliction of duty, which is what remiss means.

clue.text: Oriental porcelain I found by the sea, timeless

indicators.note: without time means a word meaning time is cut out of the phrase it qualifies

parts.note: taken as written
maritime means by or of the sea

explanation.surface: A collector finds some old Eastern porcelain on the shore, an ageless treasure.
explanation.walkthrough: TIME is removed from MARITIME, leaving MARI.
explanation.definitionFit: Imari is Japanese porcelain named after the port it was shipped from, so an Oriental ware.

clue.text: Type of resin discerned around spilt pail

indicators.note: around tells us the word for discerned wraps about the reworked letters

parts.note: to have got something is to have understood or discerned it

indicators.note: something spilt is scattered, so the letters of pail fall into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone notices tree sap leaking from a knocked-over bucket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Discerned' is a past tense, so its synonym is got, as in 'I got the joke'; that word goes around the scattered bucket.
explanation.definitionFit: Galipot is a crude turpentine oleoresin that hardens on the bark of certain pine trees.

clue.text: Certain categories? Lot once accepted

parts.note: an old sense of tax is a task or allotted share, one's lot
A is the abbreviation for accepted, as written on a bill of exchange

explanation.surface: An auction lot from the past that was finally accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Lot' suggests an auction; 'once' flags an obsolete meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Taxa are the groups biologists classify living things into, such as species and genera: particular categories.

clue.text: A rude rep out of order, on his high horse?

indicators.note: things out of order are not in their proper sequence, so these letters need rearranging

parts.note: the letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A rude sales rep is being pompous and superior.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks the definition as playful: someone on a high horse is literally raised up.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider on a tall horse is lifted aloft, so upreared, meaning raised up, fits the literal reading of the idiom.

clue.text: Affluent rulers, smart, left court rolling within

indicators.note: within places the tumbled letters inside the word for smart

parts.note: smart in the sense of brisk, as in a smart pace, is pacy

indicators.note: rolling means tumbling over, so the letters for left and court are turned into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Wealthy, stylish rulers leave a royal court that is awash with money.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Smart' here is brisk, as in a smart pace, not stylish; 'rolling' in the surface hints at rolling in money but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A plutocracy is government by the wealthy, or the wealthy class who rule.

clue.text: Radical in medley creating super record

indicators.note: in places the first word inside the second

parts.note: a mingle is a mixture or medley
radical means of the root, and in botany the axis is the central root-and-stem line of a plant

explanation.surface: A radical musician mixes a medley into a great new record.
explanation.walkthrough: Mingle is a rare noun meaning a mixture; 'Radical' leans on its root sense, as the radix or axis of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A maxi-single is a single carrying extra tracks, so a bigger-than-usual record.

clue.text: Health, disposing of last two bumped off

indicators.note: getting rid of the final pair means the end of the word is chopped off

parts.note: sláinte is the Gaelic toast meaning 'health!'

explanation.surface: A toast to good health, ironically followed by two people being killed.
explanation.walkthrough: The toast loses its final two letters TE.
explanation.definitionFit: To bump off is slang for to kill, so bumped off means murdered, slain.

clue.text: To macerate, man cut with chopper

indicators.note: cut means docked at the end, so the word loses its last letter

parts.note: a man is a male
ax is the American spelling of axe, a chopping tool

explanation.surface: A man chops food with a chopper to soften it up.
explanation.definitionFit: Malax is an old verb meaning to soften by kneading or rubbing, which is what macerate means.

clue.text: After temperature, aunt's treated — some thought it cured anything

indicators.note: after puts the reworked letters behind the abbreviation for temperature
treated means processed or worked on, so these letters are reworked into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A feverish aunt gets medical care from a supposed cure-all.
explanation.walkthrough: T (temperature), then 'treated' rearranges AUNT'S into UTSAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Tutsan, a kind of St John's wort, takes its name from French toute-saine, all-healthy, as it was once thought a universal remedy.

clue.text: Cross letters, cross one following up in the heat of the moment (6, two words)

definitions.text: in the heat of the moment

parts.note: the initials of Iesus Nazarenus Rex Iudaeorum inscribed on the Cross
an X is a cross
a means one

explanation.surface: An angry letter-writer fires off cross letters, one after another, while still worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cross' is used twice: first for the inscription on Christ's Cross, then for the letter X. In rixa is Latin for 'in a quarrel'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin phrase means during a brawl or quarrel, when tempers are hot.

clue.text: Mow middle of pitch when sun is following

indicators.note: the middle of a word is its central letter, the only one kept

parts.note: the central letter of pitch
as means when, as in 'as I left'
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A groundsman mows the centre of the cricket pitch while the sun shines.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mow' looks like a verb about grass; here it is a noun, a heap of hay.
explanation.definitionFit: A mow is a stack of hay or grain, and tass is a dialect word for such a heap.

clue.text: Fatty stuff Greek character enclosed in cover

indicators.note: enclosed in means shut inside, so the letter goes within the other word

parts.note: a lid is a cover
pi is a letter of the Greek alphabet

explanation.surface: A greasy Greek character hides under a cover.
explanation.definitionFit: Lipids are the class of fats and oily substances in living cells.

clue.text: Mixed studies with time seen as extremely old-fashioned

indicators.note: mixed means jumbled together, so these letters come out in a new order

parts.note: taken as written
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: Mixed studies over time come to look very outdated.
explanation.definitionFit: Dusty means stale and antiquated, so the superlative describes the most old-fashioned.

clue.text: Dead head giving one a sinking sensation

parts.note: gone means dead
a ness is a headland

explanation.surface: A dead head is a gruesome find that makes one feel queasy.
explanation.definitionFit: Goneness is a faint, hollow feeling of weakness, as when the stomach sinks.

clue.text: Pacific islander unchanged after being brought up

definitions.text: Pacific islander unchanged after being brought up

parts.words: Pacific islander unchanged after being brought up
parts.note: the islander's name, written up the grid in this down light, reads exactly as it does downwards

explanation.surface: Someone from a South Seas island has kept their character despite their upbringing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brought up' suggests upbringing, but in a down light it means read in reverse; the islander's name is a palindrome, so reversing leaves it unchanged.
explanation.definitionFit: A Nauruan is a native of Nauru, a small island republic in the western Pacific Ocean.

clue.text: Better-looking woman's one captivated after James turns up?

indicators.note: turning up in a down light means the name is read from bottom to top

parts.note: Sid James, the comic actor of the Carry On films

indicators.note: something captivated is held captive, so it sits inside the other word

parts.note: her is the possessive for a woman
Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A woman is charmed when the handsome James shows up.
explanation.walkthrough: Sid James was a much-loved British comedy actor, star of the Carry On films.
explanation.definitionFit: Dishy is British slang for attractive, so dishier means more good-looking.

clue.text: Pain in the joints: is it involved with toes?

indicators.note: involved means entangled, so the letters are tangled together into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A patient asks whether the ache in the joints has to do with the toes.
explanation.definitionFit: Osteitis is inflammation of bone, a painful condition felt around the joints.

clue.text: Évian added to wine? It damages hock

parts.note: Évian-les-Bains is a French spa town
vin is French for wine

explanation.surface: Is watering down wine with mineral water a crime against a good German hock?
explanation.walkthrough: Hock seems to be the Rhine wine; it is the hock joint of a horse's hind leg.
explanation.definitionFit: Spavin is a disease of a horse's hock joint, causing swelling and lameness.

clue.text: Cadogan maybe, earl wearing 'Arry's topper uptilted

indicators.note: tilted upwards in a down light means the whole lot is read from the bottom
whoever wears a hat is inside it, so the letter goes within the headgear

parts.note: a cockney like 'Arry drops the h of top hat
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: An earl puts on a Cockney's top hat at a jaunty angle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Arry is the stock cockney who drops his aitches. A Cadogan is a lidless teapot filled through the base.
explanation.definitionFit: A Cadogan is a type of teapot, filled from underneath, so the definition is by example.

clue.text: A dependable guy? A view not universally held!

definitions.meaning: the setter's reading: an old word for a thoroughly good, reliable fellow
surface reading: a wry aside about a much-disputed American president

explanation.walkthrough: The dictionary sense is a trusty good sort; the exclamation teases that, given the famous bearer of the name, not everyone would agree.
explanation.definitionFit: In old slang a trump is a fine fellow you can rely on, like a trump card that wins the trick.

clue.text: Village head

parts.note: surface reading: the leader of a small community; the setter's reading: the title of a headman in parts of India and the Middle East

explanation.walkthrough: The clue is a bare definition of an unusual word: a malik is a chief or village headman in India and the Arab world.
explanation.definitionFit: Malik means king or chief in Arabic and is used for the headman of a village.

clue.text: Seats mostly searched from back to front

indicators.note: reading from the back to the front means the letters run in the opposite order
mostly means not quite all, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: to sweep an area is to search it thoroughly

explanation.surface: Seats in a hall are searched row by row from the back to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Pews are the long bench seats in a church.

clue.text: Explanation of Latin text (section in course)

indicators.note: in places the single letter inside the other word

parts.note: fare is food, the dishes served as a course
S is the abbreviation for section

explanation.surface: A student's crib explains a Latin passage, a section of the course.
explanation.walkthrough: The parenthesis hides the wordplay inside the definition's picture of a Latin course.
explanation.definitionFit: A farse is a vernacular gloss or interpolation inserted into a Latin liturgical text to explain it.

clue.text: Meeting in Nairobi requiring bazaar being moved

indicators.note: being moved means shifted about, so these letters change places

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A public meeting in Kenya's capital needs the market to be relocated.
explanation.definitionFit: A baraza is a Swahili word for a public meeting or council in East Africa.

clue.text: Dug round in dock

indicators.note: in places the ring shape inside the other word

parts.note: to bob a tail is to dock or cut it short
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: Someone dug a hole round the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dug' looks like the past tense of dig; it is the noun for a teat or udder.
explanation.definitionFit: A dug is an animal's teat or breast, and boob is slang for a breast.

clue.text: Desert plants, hot inside, a gila demolished

indicators.note: inside puts the letter for hot within the rearranged letters
a building demolished is knocked down, so the letters of a gila are rebuilt in another order

parts.note: taken as written
H is the standard abbreviation for hot, as on taps

explanation.surface: In the desert, a Gila monster wrecks the vegetation in the heat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demolished' rearranges A GILA into ALAGI, with H (hot) placed 'inside' after AL. A Gila monster is a venomous lizard of the American desert.
explanation.definitionFit: Alhagi is a genus of thorny shrubs, including camelthorn, that grow in arid regions.

clue.text: Oil freely edging copper round windows

indicators.note: edging means forming a border around, so the rearranged letters surround the symbol for copper
freely means without restraint, so the letters of Oil are allowed to move into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
Cu is the chemical symbol for copper

explanation.surface: Lubricant is applied liberally to the copper surround of some windows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Round' looks like part of the wordplay but belongs to the definition: these are circular windows.
explanation.definitionFit: Oculi, plural of oculus, are circular openings such as the round window at the top of a dome.

clue.text: Pour out Scotch, bitter fluid when dash of rum's included

indicators.note: included means taken inside, so the letter sits within the fluid

parts.note: bile is the bitter digestive fluid from the liver

indicators.note: a dash is a tiny amount, so just the first letter is taken

parts.note: the first letter of rum

explanation.surface: Pouring a Scotch whisky, a bitter drink once a splash of rum is added.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scotch' looks like the whisky; it labels the definition as a Scots word.
explanation.definitionFit: In Scots, to birle is to pour out drink or ply someone with it.

clue.text: Some circuits I cede so, struggling, second to finish

indicators.note: to finish puts the letter for second at the very end
struggling suggests writhing about, so these letters are twisted into a different order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A racing driver, struggling to come second, gives way on the circuit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struggling' rearranges I CEDE SO into DIOCESE, and S (second) comes 'to finish'.
explanation.definitionFit: A diocese is a bishop's district, and circuit is a word for a church's administrative area.

clue.text: Depositor receives this mound to bury, set apart (12, two words)

parts.note: a bank is a mound or ridge of earth
to inter is to bury

indicators.note: apart means the letters are broken up and reassembled

explanation.surface: A burial instruction: heap up earth, inter, and keep separate.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who leaves money in an account is paid a percentage on it by the institution holding it.
